paragraphs.text: Vitelliform macular dystrophies (VMD) are inherited retinal dystrophies with yellow, round deposits seen on fundus examination. These deposits occur in juvenile Best macular dystrophy and in adult-onset vitelliform macular dystrophy. Many cases have mutations in BEST1 or PRPH2, but the genetic cause is unknown in many affected individuals (Manes et al., 2013).

paragraphs.text: Meunier et al. (2014) found that 13 patients from 4 families with IMPG1 or IMPG2 mutations had late-onset vitelliform macular dystrophy (mean age at onset 42 years) with moderate visual impairment (mean visual acuity 20/40); the sporadic presumed recessive case in family 3 had onset at 38 years and visual acuity 20/50. Drusen-like lesions adjacent to the vitelliform deposits were seen in 9 of 13 patients. On spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT), the vitelliform material lay above a well-preserved retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) of normal reflectivity at all stages, located between the ellipsoid and interdigitation lines. EOG results were normal or borderline in 9 cases.

paragraphs.text: Brandl et al. (2017) also reported a Turkish boy, homozygous for an IMPG1 mutation, who was diagnosed with VMD at age 2 years and had fluctuating visual acuity of about 0.2 logMAR over 8 years of follow-up. At age 10, multifocal ERG was normal and the EOG Arden ratio was borderline to slightly low. Fundi showed a bilateral singular central vitelliform lesion without satellite drusen. SD-OCT showed a dome-shaped foveal detachment of the neurosensory retina with hyperreflective material that was reabsorbed, leaving an optically empty cavity, elongated photoreceptor outer segments, and preserved Bruch membrane/RPE; fundus autofluorescence hyperfluorescence decreased over time.

paragraphs.text: Brandl et al. (2017) described strikingly similar phenotypes in 10 patients with IMPG1 or IMPG2 mutations, with presumably consecutive stages: singular central vitelliform lesions with neurosensory detachment and hyperreflective material above a preserved Bruch membrane/RPE; resorption leaving a dome-shaped optically empty cavity; and collapse with central atrophy and RPE loss, causing the most pronounced vision loss. paragraphs.text: Gupta et al. (2021) described a 25-year-old woman with symptomatic scotoma and decreased vision who had small yellow spots at the fovea in both eyes. paragraphs.text: In a large family with autosomal dominant VMD, Manes et al. (2013) used gene mapping and whole-exome sequencing to identify a heterozygous c.713T-G mutation in the IMPG1 gene, resulting in a leu238-to-arg (L238R) substitution. paragraphs.text: Brandl et al. (2017) screened IMPG1 and IMPG2 in 106 unrelated patients with Best disease or adult-onset VMD who were negative for BEST1 and PRPH2 mutations, and identified IMPG1 mutations in 2 simplex cases with onset in early childhood. In a German boy (patient 1, family 13-501), they identified a heterozygous c.713T-C transition in exon 7 of IMPG1, resulting in a leu238-to-pro (L238P) substitution in the SEA I domain; he was the only affected family member and parental data were unavailable. In a boy (patient 2) from a consanguineous Turkish family (11-151), they identified a homozygous c.807+5G-A splice site mutation in intron 7 of IMPG1; both parents were heterozygous. In a minigene assay, the c.807+5G-A mutation caused skipping of exon 7 in about half of transcripts.

paragraphs.text: Olivier et al. (2021) performed exome sequencing in a family with autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa (RP) and identified a splice variant in the IMPG1 gene. The same variant was then found in individuals from 2 more families, who had either RP or VMD. Screening of 596 families with RP or VMD by gene panel testing and exome sequencing identified 8 more families carrying different missense or nonsense variants in IMPG1. The authors concluded that monoallelic or biallelic IMPG1 variants are associated with RP. They also revised the clinical diagnosis for an IMPG1 retinopathy-associated variant that had originally been described as benign concentric annular macular dystrophy, reclassifying it as RP with early macular involvement.

paragraphs.text: In a German boy (patient 1, family 13-501) with VMD4, Brandl et al. (2017) identified a heterozygous c.713T-C transition in exon 7 of the IMPG1 gene, resulting in a leu238-to-pro (L238P) substitution in the SEA I domain. The variant was predicted pathogenic by all 3 in silico algorithms used and was absent from the ExAC database. He was the only affected family member; parental data were unavailable. The authors noted that a different substitution at the same residue (L238R) had previously been reported in autosomal dominant VMD and suggested a dominant-negative effect or haploinsufficiency. The patient was initially diagnosed at age 12 and at age 13 had reduced visual acuity, with central RPE abnormalities and foveal detachment in both fundi.

paragraphs.text: In a boy (patient 2) from a consanguineous Turkish family (11-151) with VMD4 diagnosed at age 2 years, Brandl et al. (2017) identified a homozygous c.807+5G-A splice site mutation in intron 7 of the IMPG1 gene; both parents were heterozygous. In a minigene assay in HEK293 cells, the mutation caused skipping of exon 7 in about half of transcripts, which was predicted to lead to nonsense-mediated decay. The heterozygous parents (aged 35 and 40 years) were asymptomatic with normal multimodal retinal imaging; the authors suggested that the residual correctly spliced transcript is sufficient to prevent subclinical abnormalities in carriers.
